uncited: Ray-tetrahedron intersection determines the entry and exit points of a ray as it traverses a tetrahedral cell, which is the fundamental geometric primitive for rendering unstructured volumetric data.

It solves the problem of efficiently computing the intersection segment $[t_{enter}, t_{exit}]$ required for volume integration, distinguishing itself from sibling methods by handling the specific topology of four triangular faces and the potential for non-convex or deformed geometries.
The problem of ray-tetrahedron intersection is central to the visualization of unstructured grid data, such as that produced by finite element analysis (FEA) or computational fluid dynamics (CFD).

Early methods relied on decomposing the tetrahedron into four triangles and applying ray-triangle intersection tests, such as the Möller–Trumbore algorithm, which is computationally redundant due to shared edges.
This approach leverages the topological connectivity of the tetrahedron to enable early termination and shared edge computations.
